ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A small lunar lander is connected to the space station, and together they make circular motion around the Moon. Its orbital radius is 3 times the radius of the Moon. At a certain moment, the space station makes the lunar lander decelerate and separate. The lunar lander lands on the Moon along the elliptical orbit shown in the figure. After staying on the lunar surface for a period of time to complete scientific investigation work, it quickly starts and still returns along the original elliptical orbit. When it first returns to the separation point, it just docks with the space station. The rapid start time of the lunar lander can be ignored. During the whole process, the space station keeps running around the Moon in the original orbit. It is known that the gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface is g, and the radius of the Moon is R. Ignoring the influence of the Moon's rotation, the shortest time that the lunar lander can stay on the Moon is approximately (　　)
ready1_open_rewrite.title: Multi-Physics open-ended question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: It is known that the small lunar lander and the space station initially orbit the Moon together in a circular orbit with a radius 3 times the Moon's radius. At a certain moment, the lunar lander slows down and separates, landing on the Moon along the elliptical orbit shown in the figure; after staying on the lunar surface for a period of time, it quickly starts again and returns along the original elliptical orbit, and when it first returns to the separation point, it just docks with the space station that is still operating in the original circular orbit. It is known that the gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface is g, and the Moon's radius is R. Without considering the influence of the Moon's rotation, approximately how much is the shortest time that the lunar lander can stay on the Moon?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: It is known that the small lunar lander and the space station initially orbit the Moon together in a circular orbit with a radius 3 times the Moon's radius. At a certain moment, the lunar lander slows down and separates, landing on the Moon along the elliptical orbit shown in the figure; after staying on the lunar surface for a period of time, it quickly starts again and returns along the original elliptical orbit, and when it first returns to the separation point, it just docks with the space station that is still operating in the original circular orbit. It is known that the gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface is g, and the Moon's radius is R. Without considering the influence of the Moon's rotation, approximately how much is the shortest time that the lunar lander can stay on the Moon?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The gray disk in the figure represents the Moon, and outside there is a larger circular orbit centered on the Moon. The small black rectangle at the top represents the space station/separation point. There is also an elliptical orbit in the figure; it intersects the outer circular orbit at the top at the separation point, and is tangent to the lunar surface near the Moon's surface, indicating that after the lunar lander slows down from the outer circular orbit, it descends to the lunar surface along this elliptical orbit, and then returns to the separation point along the same elliptical orbit. Reasoning: The gravitational acceleration on the lunar surface is g, and the radius is R, so the lunar gravitational parameter satisfies μ/R^2=g, that is, μ=gR^2. The radius of the circular orbit where the space station is located is r_c=3R, and its period is T_c=2π√(r_c^3/μ)=2π√((3R)^3/(gR^2))=6π√3√(R/g). From the figure it can be seen that the apolune of the lunar-landing ellipse is at the separation point, at a distance 3R from the Moon's center; the perilune is on the lunar surface, at a distance R from the Moon's center. Therefore the semi-major axis of the ellipse is a=(3R+R)/2=2R. The period of the elliptical orbit is T_e=2π√(a^3/μ)=2π√((2R)^3/(gR^2))=4π√2√(R/g). The lunar lander uses half an elliptical period from the separation point to the lunar surface, and then uses another half elliptical period to return from the lunar surface to the separation point, so the total round-trip flight time is T_e. If the time staying on the lunar surface is t, then when it first returns to the separation point, in order to meet the space station that is still operating in the circular orbit, the space station must just have returned to that separation point, that is, T_e+t=nT_c. Because T_e<T_c, to make t the shortest and nonnegative, take n=1, obtaining t_min=T_c-T_e=(6√3-4√2)π√(R/g). Numerically, 6√3-4√2≈4.7, so final answer: t_min≈4.7π√(R/g).
